In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''chi distribution''' is a continuous [[probability distribution]] over the non-negative real line. It is the distribution of the positive square root of a sum of squared independent [[Normal distribution|Gaussian random variables]]. Equivalently, it is the distribution of the [[Euclidean distance]] between a multivariate Gaussian random variable and the origin. The chi distribution describes the positive square roots of a variable obeying a [[chi-squared distribution]].

If <math>Z_1, \ldots, Z_k</math> are <math>k</math> independent, [[normal distribution|normally distributed]] random variables with mean 0 and [[standard deviation]] 1, then the statistic
:<math>Y = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^k Z_i^2} </math>

is distributed according to the chi distribution. The chi distribution has one positive integer parameter <math>k</math>, which specifies the [[Degrees of freedom (statistics)|degrees of freedom]] (i.e. the number of random variables <math>Z_i</math>).

The most familiar examples are the [[Rayleigh distribution]] (chi distribution with two [[degrees of freedom]]) and the [[Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution]] of the molecular speeds in an [[ideal gas]] (chi distribution with three degrees of freedom).

== Definitions ==

=== Probability density function ===
The [[probability density function]] (pdf) of the chi-distribution is
:<math>f(x;k) = \begin{cases}
\dfrac{x^{k-1}e^{-x^2/2}}{2^{k/2-1}\Gamma\left(\frac{k}{2}\right)}, & x\geq 0; \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
</math>

where <math>\Gamma(z)</math> is the [[gamma function]].

===Cumulative distribution function===
The cumulative distribution function is given by:

:<math>F(x;k)=P(k/2,x^2/2)\,</math>

where <math>P(k,x)</math> is the [[Incomplete gamma function#Regularized gamma functions and Poisson random variables|regularized gamma function]].

===Generating functions===

The [[moment-generating function]] is given by:

:<math>M(t)=M\left(\frac{k}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{t^2}{2}\right)+t\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\Gamma((k+1)/2)}{\Gamma(k/2)} M\left(\frac{k+1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{t^2}{2}\right),</math>

where <math>M(a,b,z)</math> is Kummer's [[confluent hypergeometric function]]. The [[Characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] is given by:

:<math>\varphi(t;k)=M\left(\frac{k}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{-t^2}{2}\right) + it\sqrt{2}\,\frac{\Gamma((k+1)/2)}{\Gamma(k/2)} M\left(\frac{k+1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{-t^2}{2}\right).</math>

==Properties==

=== Moments ===
The raw [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] are then given by:

:<math>\mu_j = \int_0^\infty f(x;k) x^j \mathrm{d} x = 2^{j/2}\ \frac{\ \Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}(k+j) \right)\ }{\Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}k \right)}</math>

where <math>\ \Gamma(z)\ </math> is the [[gamma function]]. Thus the first few raw moments are:

:<math>\mu_1 = \sqrt{2\ }\ \frac{\ \Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}(k + 1) \right)\ }{\Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}k \right)}</math>
:<math>\mu_2 = k\ ,</math>
:<math>\mu_3=2\sqrt{2\ }\ \frac{\ \Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}(k + 3) \right)\ }{\Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}k \right)} = (k+1)\ \mu_1\ ,</math> 
:<math>\mu_4 = (k)(k+2)\ ,</math>
:<math>\mu_5 = 4\sqrt{2\ }\ \frac{\ \Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}(k\!+\!5) \right)\ }{\Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}k \right)} = (k+1)(k+3)\ \mu_1\ ,</math>
:<math> \mu_6 = (k)(k+2)(k+4)\ ,</math>

where the rightmost expressions are derived using the recurrence relationship for the gamma function:

:<math> \Gamma(x+1) = x\ \Gamma(x) ~.</math>

From these expressions we may derive the following relationships:

Mean: <math> \mu = \sqrt{2\ }\ \frac{\ \Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2}(k+1) \right)\ }{\Gamma\left( \tfrac{1}{2} k \right)}\ ,</math> which is close to <math> \sqrt{k - \tfrac{1}{2}\ }\ </math> for large {{mvar|k}}.

Variance: <math> V = k - \mu^2\ ,</math> which approaches <math>\ \tfrac{1}{2}\ </math> as {{mvar|k}} increases.

Skewness: <math> \gamma_1 = \frac{\mu}{\ \sigma^3\ } \left(1 - 2 \sigma^2 \right) ~.</math>

Kurtosis excess: <math>\gamma_2 = \frac{2}{\ \sigma^2\ } \left(1 - \mu\ \sigma\ \gamma_1 - \sigma^2 \right) ~.</math>

===Entropy===
The entropy is given by:

:<math>S=\ln(\Gamma(k/2))+\frac{1}{2}(k\!-\!\ln(2)\!-\!(k\!-\!1)\psi^0(k/2))</math>

where <math>\psi^0(z)</math> is the [[polygamma function]].

===Large n approximation===
We find the large n=k+1 approximation of the mean and variance of chi distribution. This has application e.g. in finding the distribution of standard deviation of a sample of normally distributed population, where n is the sample size.

The mean is then:
:<math>\mu = \sqrt{2}\,\,\frac{\Gamma(n/2)}{\Gamma((n-1)/2)}</math>
We use the [[Multiplication theorem#Gamma function–Legendre formula|Legendre duplication formula]] to write:
:<math>2^{n-2} \,\Gamma((n-1)/2)\cdot \Gamma(n/2) = \sqrt{\pi} \Gamma (n-1)</math>,
so that:
:<math>\mu = \sqrt{2/\pi}\,2^{n-2}\,\frac{(\Gamma(n/2))^2}{\Gamma(n-1)}</math>
Using [[Stirling's approximation]] for Gamma function, we get the following expression for the mean:
:<math>\mu = \sqrt{2/\pi}\,2^{n-2}\,\frac{\left(\sqrt{2\pi}(n/2-1)^{n/2-1+1/2}e^{-(n/2-1)}\cdot[1+\frac{1}{12(n/2-1)}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})]\right)^2}{\sqrt{2\pi}(n-2)^{n-2+1/2}e^{-(n-2)}\cdot [1+\frac{1}{12(n-2)}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})]}</math>
::<math> = (n-2)^{1/2}\,\cdot \left[1+\frac{1}{4n}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})\right] = \sqrt{n-1}\,(1-\frac{1}{n-1})^{1/2}\cdot \left[1+\frac{1}{4n}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})\right]</math>
::<math> = \sqrt{n-1}\,\cdot \left[1-\frac{1}{2n}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})\right]\,\cdot \left[1+\frac{1}{4n}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})\right]</math>
::<math> = \sqrt{n-1}\,\cdot \left[1-\frac{1}{4n}+O(\frac{1}{n^2})\right]</math>
And thus the variance is:
:<math>V=(n-1)-\mu^2\, = (n-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2n}\,\cdot \left[1+O(\frac{1}{n})\right] = \frac12 + O(\frac1n)</math>

==Related distributions==
*If <math>X \sim \chi_k</math> then <math>X^2 \sim \chi^2_k</math> ([[chi-squared distribution]])
*<math> \chi_1 \sim \mathrm{HN}(1)\,</math> ([[half-normal distribution]]), i.e. if <math> X \sim N(0,1)\,</math> then <math>| X | \sim \chi_1 \,</math>, and if <math>Y \sim \mathrm{HN}(\sigma)\,</math> for any <math> \sigma > 0 \, </math> then <math>\tfrac{Y}{\sigma} \sim \chi_1\,</math> 
*<math> \chi_2 \sim \mathrm{Rayleigh}(1)\,</math> ([[Rayleigh distribution]]) and if <math>Y \sim \mathrm{Rayleigh}(\sigma)\,</math> for any <math> \sigma > 0 \, </math> then <math>\tfrac{Y}{\sigma} \sim \chi_2\,</math> 
*<math> \chi_3 \sim \mathrm{Maxwell}(1)\,</math> ([[Maxwell distribution]]) and if <math>Y \sim \mathrm{Maxwell}(a)\,</math> for any <math> a > 0 \, </math> then <math>\tfrac{Y}{a} \sim \chi_3\,</math> 
*<math> \|\boldsymbol{N}_{i=1,\ldots,k}{(0,1)}\|_2 \sim \chi_k </math>, the [[Norm (mathematics)#Euclidean norm|Euclidean norm]] of a [[Multivariate normal distribution#Standard normal random vector|standard normal random vector]] of with <math>k</math> dimensions, is distributed according to a chi distribution with <math> k </math> [[Degrees of freedom (statistics)|degrees of freedom]]
*chi distribution is a special case of various distributions: [[generalized gamma distribution|generalized gamma]], [[Nakagami distribution|Nakagami]], [[noncentral chi distribution|noncentral chi]], etc.
*<math> \lim_{k \to \infty}\tfrac{\chi_k-\mu_k}{\sigma_k}  \xrightarrow{d}\ N(0,1) \,</math> ([[Normal distribution]])
*The mean of the chi distribution (scaled by the square root of <math>n-1</math>) yields the correction factor in the [[Unbiased estimation of standard deviation#Results for the normal distribution|unbiased estimation of the standard deviation of the normal distribution]].
